catalog_quote: For describing the placement of stress in feet (4.), it is convenient to distinguish high and low syllables. High syllables contain at least one vowel with high tone; low syllables do not. For the same purpose, long and short vowels are distinguished: long syllables contain more than one vowel; short syllables do not. ... The foot is a rhythm unit bounded by slight decreases in tempo and including one stressed syllable. Stressed syllables have greater intensity or greater duration, or both, than unstressed syllables of comparable segmental composition. The placement of stress within a foot is predictable on the basis of the distribution of long and high syllables (defined at the end of 3.) in that foot. If a foot contains a long syllable (and no foot contains more than one long syllable), that syllable is stressed. Otherwise, the first high syllable of the foot is stressed. In feet with…

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Huttar & Huttar 1972 scan at the stated pages (pp. 4-6, rule on p. 6). The source is a primary phonology paper by the language's principal describers, so the weight-hedged/QS-HEDGED coding (long syllable stressed within the foot, else tone-conditioned, else penult) is directly supported, and the carried 1994:565 passage from the same authors agrees on the weight clause ('If there is a heavy syllable in the word it carries the stress'). It is not 'well-sourced' because the authoritative 631-pp 1994 Routledge grammar is not held and its passage is known only through StressTyp2; ST1's note that heavy = long vowels AND closed syllables, plus 'many exceptions' and the remark that the authors may conflate prominence and stress, means reading pp. 565-567 directly could refine wcls (CVV -> CVV+CVN) and the default-position wording, but
